## Setup

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
```

## Question 1: New Jersey's individual market, 2000 to 2008

### (a) Build the dataset

The dataset comes from the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance
Individual Health Coverage (IHC) data. For each year from 2000 to 2008, it has
the monthly family premium for Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield Plan D (\$1,000
deductible), Aetna Plan D (\$1,000 deductible), and Celtic Plan C (\$2,500
deductible), along with total year-end standard enrollment in the IHC program.
The file is `nj-ihc.csv` at the top of this repository, outside the gitignored
`data/` folder so that it is included in the submission.

```{r}
nj <- read_csv("../nj-ihc.csv")

kable(nj, format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
      col.names = c("Year", "BCBS Plan D", "Aetna Plan D", "Celtic Plan C",
                    "Enrollment"),
      caption = "Monthly family premiums ($) and year-end standard enrollment, NJ IHC")
```

### (b) Make the figure

Premiums and enrollment are in different units, so the figure shows them in two
panels over the same years.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
nj_long <- bind_rows(
  nj %>%
    pivot_longer(c(bcbs_plan_d, aetna_plan_d, celtic_plan_c),
                 names_to = "series", values_to = "value") %>%
    mutate(panel = "Monthly family premium ($)",
           series = recode(series, bcbs_plan_d = "BCBS Plan D",
                           aetna_plan_d = "Aetna Plan D",
                           celtic_plan_c = "Celtic Plan C")),
  nj %>%
    transmute(year, series = "Enrollment", value = enrollment,
              panel = "Year-end standard enrollment")
)

ggplot(nj_long, aes(year, value, group = series)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(data = nj_long %>% filter(year == 2008, series != "Enrollment"),
            aes(label = series), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2000:2008, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.18))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL,
       title = "NJ individual market: premiums rise as enrollment falls") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
first <- nj %>% filter(year == 2000)
last <- nj %>% filter(year == 2008)
```

All three premiums rise sharply over the period. The BCBS Plan D premium goes
from \$`r comma(first$bcbs_plan_d)` a month in 2000 to
\$`r comma(last$bcbs_plan_d)` in 2008, about
`r round(last$bcbs_plan_d / first$bcbs_plan_d, 1)` times as high. Aetna rises
from \$`r comma(first$aetna_plan_d)` to \$`r comma(last$aetna_plan_d)`, and
Celtic from \$`r comma(first$celtic_plan_c)` to \$`r comma(last$celtic_plan_c)`,
with Celtic's premium unchanged from 2003 on. Over the same years, year-end
enrollment falls every year, from `r comma(first$enrollment)` to
`r comma(last$enrollment)`, a decline of about
`r percent(1 - last$enrollment / first$enrollment)`.

### (c) Interpret it

Rising premiums together with falling enrollment is what adverse selection
predicts. The IHC program was guaranteed issue and community rated, so insurers
had to accept every applicant and charge everyone in a plan the same premium.
When premiums rise, the people most likely to drop coverage are the healthiest,
who expect to use the least care and so get the least value from insurance. Their
exit leaves a sicker and more expensive pool, which raises the insurer's average
cost and leads to another premium increase the next year, and the cycle repeats.

### (d) Verdict

Other forces could produce part of this pattern. Health care costs rose across
the whole economy in the 2000s, so some of the premium growth would have happened
without any change in who was enrolled. The IHC market is also small, so a change
by a single insurer, such as a new plan design or a decision to stop marketing a
plan, can move premiums and enrollment on its own.

Even so, the size of the changes points to selection. The BCBS Plan D premium
rose about 4.5 times in eight years. By comparison, the average employer premium
for family coverage rose 119% from 1999 to 2008, a little more than doubling
([KFF Employer Health Benefits 2008 Annual Survey](https://www.kff.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/04/7790.pdf)). Meanwhile,
enrollment fell by nearly half and kept falling every year. That combination is
hard to explain without healthier people leaving the pool. I read it as a death
spiral in progress, a market unraveling steadily rather than collapsing at once,
since `r comma(last$enrollment)` people were still enrolled in 2008.

## Question 2: Medicare Advantage and fee-for-service, 2008 to 2023

### (a) Build the national series

```{r}
pen <- read_csv("../data/medicare-ma-penetration.csv", col_types = cols(fips = "c"))
ffs <- read_csv("../data/medicare-ffs-costs.csv", col_types = cols(fips = "c"))
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_pen <- nrow(pen)
n_ffs <- nrow(ffs)
na_ma <- sum(is.na(pen$ma_enrolled))
na_ffs <- sum(is.na(ffs$ffs_enrollment) | is.na(ffs$ffs_spending))
```

Both files have one row per county and year, identified by the county FIPS code.
The penetration file has `r comma(n_pen)` rows and the FFS file has
`r comma(n_ffs)`. A few rows have missing values. There are `r na_ma`
county-years with no reported MA enrollment, which I treat as zero, and
`r na_ffs` with missing FFS enrollment or spending, which I drop.

```{r}
pen <- pen %>% mutate(ma_enrolled = replace_na(ma_enrolled, 0))
ffs <- ffs %>% filter(!is.na(ffs_enrollment), !is.na(ffs_spending))

county <- pen %>%
  select(fips, year, total_eligibles, ma_enrolled) %>%
  inner_join(ffs %>% select(fips, year, ffs_enrollment, ffs_spending),
             by = c("fips", "year"), relationship = "one-to-one")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n_county <- nrow(county)
```

The merged file has `r comma(n_county)` county-years. A national rate is not the
average of the county rates, because that would give a small rural county the same
weight as Los Angeles. Instead, I add up the counts across counties in each year
and then divide. National MA penetration is total MA enrollment over total
eligibles, and FFS spending per enrollee is total FFS spending over total FFS
enrollment. Spending is converted to numeric before summing, since national FFS
spending runs to hundreds of billions of dollars, beyond the largest value R can
hold as an integer.

```{r}
national <- county %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(ma_penetration = sum(ma_enrolled) / sum(total_eligibles),
            ffs_per_enrollee = sum(as.numeric(ffs_spending)) / sum(ffs_enrollment))

kable(national %>%
        mutate(ma_penetration = percent(ma_penetration, accuracy = 0.1),
               ffs_per_enrollee = dollar(ffs_per_enrollee, accuracy = 1)),
      col.names = c("Year", "MA penetration", "FFS spending per enrollee"),
      caption = "National MA penetration and FFS spending per enrollee")
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
national %>%
  transmute(year,
            `MA penetration (%)` = 100 * ma_penetration,
            `FFS spending per enrollee ($)` = ffs_per_enrollee) %>%
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, value)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2008, 2023, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL,
       title = "MA penetration and FFS spending per enrollee, 2008 to 2023") +
  theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#| include: false
n08 <- national %>% filter(year == 2008)
n16 <- national %>% filter(year == 2016)
n23 <- national %>% filter(year == 2023)
```

MA penetration rises every year, from
`r percent(n08$ma_penetration, accuracy = 0.1)` of eligibles in 2008 to
`r percent(n23$ma_penetration, accuracy = 0.1)` in 2023, and it rises faster
after 2018. FFS spending per enrollee, in nominal dollars, is nearly flat from
2008 to 2016, at `r dollar(n08$ffs_per_enrollee, accuracy = 1)` and
`r dollar(n16$ffs_per_enrollee, accuracy = 1)`. It then rises to
`r dollar(n23$ffs_per_enrollee, accuracy = 1)` by 2023, with a dip in 2020, when
the COVID pandemic disrupted care, and a jump in 2021.

### (b) Read them together

The two series are consistent with healthier, lower-cost beneficiaries moving
into Medicare Advantage and sicker, higher-cost beneficiaries staying in
fee-for-service. As healthier people leave traditional Medicare, the people who
remain are more expensive on average, which pushes up FFS spending per enrollee.
This is adverse selection in the choice between two kinds of coverage rather than
in the choice of whether to insure at all. The national series cannot establish
selection on its own, however. FFS spending per enrollee also moves with medical
prices and use, and it was nearly flat for most of the 2010s even as penetration
kept rising, so the two series do not move together year by year.

### (c) Risk adjustment

Medicare pays an MA plan a fixed monthly amount for each enrollee. Risk adjustment
scales that payment to the enrollee's expected cost, using a risk score built from
age, sex, and recorded diagnoses, so a plan is paid more for a sicker enrollee and
less for a healthier one. The problem it addresses is the selection in part (b).
With a flat payment per person, a plan would profit from attracting healthy
enrollees and avoiding sick ones. Tying payment to expected cost reduces that
reward, so plans have less reason to compete by choosing whom they enroll. Risk
adjustment is imperfect, however. Because payment depends on recorded diagnoses,
plans have an incentive to record diagnoses more completely, which raises risk
scores and payments without enrollees being any sicker.

### (d) Beyond risk adjustment

One policy aimed at holding down fee-for-service costs is the Medicare Shared
Savings Program, which pays accountable care organizations (ACOs). An ACO is a
group of physicians, hospitals, and other providers that agrees to be held
accountable for the total spending and quality of care of the traditional
Medicare beneficiaries assigned to it. Providers are still paid fee-for-service,
but if the ACO's spending comes in below a benchmark and it meets quality
standards, it keeps a share of the savings, and in some arrangements it owes
Medicare part of any spending above the benchmark. That gives providers in
traditional Medicare a reason to avoid unnecessary care, which they lack under
fee-for-service alone
([MedPAC, "Accountable Care Organization Payment Systems," Payment Basics, October 2024](https://www.medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/MedPAC_Payment_Basics_24_ACOs_FINAL_SEC.pdf)).
